summary: Recent documents have discussed how hard it is to identify hosts in address-sharing systems such as carrier-grade NATs and proxies. This experimental memo describes the design, deployment and privacy considerations of a TCP option that reveals a host identifier in such deployments.

eli5.summary: When many houses share a single street number, it is hard to tell who is knocking. This experiment adds a small tag to connections so the receiver can tell the real sender apart.

questions: what is the tcp host id option
why do we need to identify hosts behind nat
subtitle: A TCP option to identify individual hosts behind address-sharing devices.

tldr.problem: When multiple hosts share a single IP address through carrier-grade NATs or proxies, the receiving server cannot distinguish which host sent a particular message. This makes it hard to apply per-host policies or identify attack sources.
tldr.mechanism: A TCP option called HOST_ID carries a host identifier value chosen by the address-sharing device. The device inserts this value to reveal information about the original sender while keeping the value opaque to the receiver.
tldr.outcome: The option is already widely deployed on the public Internet, but the IETF rejected it as a permanent standard due to privacy and technical concerns. It remains experimental.

today: RFC 7974 is published as Informational. The IETF rejected it for a permanent standard due to privacy and technical concerns, but it is widely deployed on the public Internet by Content Delivery Networks and other operators. It remains experimental and is not eligible for an assigned TCP option codepoint.

sections.title: Why Host Identification Matters
sections.content:
The Internet was built assuming each computer has its own IP address. But today, many devices share a single address through address-sharing systems like carrier-grade NATs (which allow a network operator to translate many private addresses into one public address) and application proxies (which relay connections between two networks).

When a server receives a connection from a shared address, it cannot tell which of the many hosts actually sent it. This breaks security policies (you cannot block an attacker without blocking legitimate users), load balancing (you cannot spread clients across servers fairly), and subscriber billing (you cannot track per-subscriber bandwidth).

RFC 6967 analyzed possible solutions. A TCP option was identified as practical and safe compared to IP-layer approaches, prompting this experimental deployment memo.
sections.eli5: If many families share one street address, the mailman cannot tell which family sent a package. Adding a house number to the envelope solves this.

sections.title: Option Format
sections.content:
The HOST_ID option uses the TCP experimental option mechanism defined in RFC 6994. It carries four fields:

The option kind is 253, signaling an experimental option. The length varies based on the identifier size (a 2-byte HOST_ID needs a 6-byte option; a 4-byte HOST_ID needs an 8-byte option). The experiment ID (ExID) is 0x0348 (840 in decimal), registered with IANA. The remaining bytes hold the HOST_ID value itself.

The option value can be any identifier the address-sharing device chooses: a unique local ID that the device maps to each original host, the original host's IP address, or a combination of IP address and port number. The exact format is opaque to the receiver.
sections.eli5: The TCP option is a small tag added to packets. It contains a number or identifier that the address-sharing device picks to mark which host inside its network sent the packet.

sections.title: When and How to Use the Option
sections.content:
Only devices that change IP addresses or ports (NATs, proxies, overlay networks) may insert this option. A regular router that just forwards packets MUST NOT add or modify it.

The option MUST appear in both the initial SYN packet and all subsequent packets until the connection is fully established on the receiver, because the receiver might use SYN cookies and need the HOST_ID value to match it back to an earlier request.

When multiple address-sharing devices sit in series (for example, a client's traffic passes through a carrier-grade NAT, then an overlay network), each device may insert its own HOST_ID. Some devices preserve earlier HOST_ID options, while others replace them with their own, depending on whether they use locally unique IDs or the original host's address.

The receiving side interprets multiple HOST_ID options by concatenating them as a single large identifier.
sections.eli5: The address-sharing device adds this tag to outgoing packets so the server knows which internal host sent them. It stops adding the tag once the connection is working.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Trade-Offs
sections.content:
This option reflects a fundamental tension: address sharing hides identity, but sometimes servers need to distinguish individual hosts. The HOST_ID option exposes information that was already visible inside the address-sharing network, making it available to outside servers.

The RFC sets strict rules to limit privacy risk: the HOST_ID value MUST only reflect information that was visible in the original packets (you cannot add derived data like geographic location). It MUST change whenever the original IP address changes (no persistent global identifiers). It MUST NOT be used for trust relationships like billing without cryptographic proof.

The RFC prohibits address-sharing devices at the border between private LANs and the Internet from using this option, since anonymity is their intended purpose. Devices providing anonymity (like VPNs or Tor) MUST strip the option from packets they forward.

The IETF and IESG expressed serious concerns about pervasive monitoring. While the option does not add information beyond what the original packets contained, it makes internal addresses visible to external servers at scale, which the IETF considered undesirable.
sections.eli5: This option trades privacy for usefulness. It is only meant to show information that the server could already see if there was no sharing device. But it can enable servers to track which individual you are, so it must be used carefully.

sections.title: Interaction with Other TCP Options
sections.content:
TCP packets have a fixed 40-byte limit for all options combined. Modern operating systems pack options for MSS, window scaling, SACK, and timestamps into 19-24 bytes. Multipath TCP adds another 16 bytes. This leaves 9-21 bytes for HOST_ID in typical cases, but only 4 bytes in the tightest scenarios, which is too little for a useful HOST_ID (6 bytes minimum).

Multipath TCP (MPTCP) and HOST_ID often cannot coexist in a single SYN packet due to space pressure. Existing deployments treat them as mutually exclusive.

TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) protects the source IP address in its Message Authentication Code, making it incompatible with address sharing. Only if TCP-AO-NAT (an extension for NAT traversal) is in use can both be deployed together.

TCP Fast Open (TFO) has variable cookie sizes that can consume 6-18 bytes of option space. If a TFO cookie is longer than 13 bytes, there is no room for HOST_ID. Some deployments configure shorter cookies or treat TFO and HOST_ID as mutually exclusive.
sections.eli5: TCP packets can only carry so much extra information. HOST_ID competes for space with other useful features like multipath TCP and fast-open cookies. Sometimes you have to choose which one to use.
